P001Pragmatic Engineerpublic text

Why techies leave Big Tech

Gergely Orosz · 2024-10-15

Collects engineers’ and leaders’ accounts of leaving large companies for reasons including learning, autonomy, career progression, layoffs and compensation.

Jobs & rolesSkills & learning

Practice classification

Outside the operational-practice scope. The retained summary describes reasons for leaving employers. It does not specify an engineering learning, enablement or workflow intervention that can be linked to a particular practice without inventing one.

The record remains in the Atlas. This disposition concerns its fit to the operational practices, not its overall quality or relevance.

Review scope and coverage →
Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundary Public availability does not imply an independent check of every paragraph or chart. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Reported findings / argument. Reveals multiple motivations and trade-offs behind departures; the cases cannot estimate attrition prevalence or an AI-driven employment effect.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — practitioner interview synthesis

Editorial use. Departure accounts illuminate career fit and learning opportunities; they do not isolate AI-driven displacement.

P002Pragmatic Engineerpublic text

Did Automattic commit open source theft?

Gergely Orosz · 2024-10-18

Discusses the WordPress plugin-directory dispute, distinguishing permission to fork source from control over a distribution channel and its existing users.

Engineering structureCode quality & security

Related practices

PAT:034 Safety and Guardrails: Verification Is Not AuthorizationInforms practice · primary reading
Why these practices (1)
  • PAT:034 · Informs practice

    The distinction between permission to fork and control of a distribution channel informs checking authorization for each intended effect rather than inferring it from another permission. The dispute is not adjudicated here, and the association supplies no legal conclusion or tested agent-control design.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundaryUpdated 19 October 2024. Disputed motivations and legal characterizations are attributed, not adjudicated. This non-Pulse-titled blog article is an excerpt of a Pulse issue originally published 2024-10-17. It passes the literal title-prefix rule; it is excluded by the optional stricter Pulse-origin filter. The parent issue is provenance only, not another P article. Public availability does not imply an independent check of every paragraph or chart. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Reported findings / argument. Useful as an ecosystem-governance and dependency-trust case. The headline is an argumentative question, not a legal finding of theft.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — reported governance commentary

Editorial use. The dispute concerns authority over software distribution and dependencies; retain contested legal characterizations as allegations.

P003Pragmatic Engineerpaid preview

State of the software engineering job market in 2024

Gergely Orosz · 2024-10-22

Combines employment-change and job-listing data to describe variation in engineering demand, seniority, geography and company hiring.

Jobs & rolesEconomics

Practice classification

Outside the operational-practice scope. The available record describes labor-market demand by population and geography. Proprietary coverage and a restricted remainder provide no concrete engineering-practice decision beyond general market context.

The record remains in the Atlas. This disposition concerns its fit to the operational practices, not its overall quality or relevance.

Review scope and coverage →
Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundaryLive Data Technologies and TrueUp use proprietary coverage; TrueUp explicitly concentrates on Big Tech and selected startups. Subscriber-only article remainder not reviewed. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Reported findings / argument. The visible analysis stresses a changed market, but job listings and inferred employment changes measure different populations and do not isolate an AI effect.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — industry observational data analysis

Editorial use. Hiring and employment indicators contextualize AI-era labor claims without identifying an AI treatment effect.

P004Pragmatic Engineerpaid preview

Hiring software engineers and engineering leaders from Big Tech (Part 1)

Gergely Orosz · 2024-10-29

Uses startup hiring accounts to examine when large-company experience transfers well and when established processes or specialized tools become liabilities.

Jobs & rolesSkills & learning

Related practices

PAT:057 Structured Enablement ProgramCautions about practice · primary reading
Why these practices (1)
  • PAT:057 · Cautions about practice

    The startup accounts identify established processes and specialized tools as possible liabilities when experience moves to a new setting. This cautions an enablement plan against treating prior-employer credentials as demonstrated local readiness; selected anonymous accounts do not estimate the competence of Big Tech employees.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundaryAnonymous, selected startup accounts; not representative estimates of Big Tech employees’ competence. Subscriber-only article remainder not reviewed. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Reported findings / argument. The accessible cases encourage assessing relevant ownership and adaptability rather than treating employer prestige as sufficient evidence of fit.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — practitioner interview synthesis

Editorial use. Transfer of experience across organizations is an onboarding and recruitment question, not proof of employer-based ability.

Review scope

Jobs & rolesVerification & review

Related practices

PAT:058 Acceptable Use PolicyInforms practice · primary reading
Why these practices (1)
  • PAT:058 · Informs practice

    Accounts of unauthorized assistance and changing interview formats inform explicitly stating what AI assistance is permitted and what evidence a candidate must supply. The public-scope synthesis of 49 selected contributors is not a representative evaluation of hiring policies.

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundary49 self-selected contributions collected through messages and forms; not a representative hiring-market sample. Subscriber-only article remainder not reviewed. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Reported findings / argument. The visible reports suggest hiring signals and verification costs are changing; projections about future interview formats remain expectations, not measured outcomes.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — qualitative practitioner survey

Editorial use. AI-mediated recruiting and candidate assessment are labor-market context; 49 volunteered accounts do not measure developer productivity, retained learning or market prevalence.

Outside the operational-practice scope. Vacancy indices and competing explanations for their decline do not establish an engineering workflow mechanism or a local adoption outcome. A practice link would conflate labor-market commentary with operational measurement.

Engineering structure

Practice classification

Outside the operational-practice scope. The retained summary concerns disputed claims about a company's internal business model. It does not provide enough operational detail to classify a software practice without importing assumptions about costs, controls or workflow.

Evidence boundaryClaims about internal operations are attributed to former staff; corporate-failure explanations remain interpretations. This non-Pulse-titled blog article is an excerpt of a Pulse issue originally published 2025-06-12. It passes the literal title-prefix rule; it is excluded by the optional stricter Pulse-origin filter. The parent issue is provenance only, not another P article. Public availability does not imply an independent check of every paragraph or chart. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Recorded summary. Investigates claims that Builder.ai was merely a human-operated substitute for AI. Former-employee accounts describe a code-generation product alongside human fulfilment; a hypothetical human-operated design is an explanatory contrast, not a verified internal architecture.

Reported findings / argument. The account challenges a simplified corporate narrative. It does not independently verify the product’s reliability, staffing, financial history or productivity.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — reported investigation

Editorial use. Industry fact-checking distinguishes reported AI code generation from human fulfilment. Neither a hypothetical architecture nor employee accounts validate a capability benchmark.

Cursor makes developers less effective?

Gergely Orosz · 2025-07-24

Discusses METR’s experienced-maintainer experiment and possible workflow explanations.

Productivity

Related practices

PAT:059 Measurement & LearningCautions about practice · primary reading
Why these practices (1)
  • PAT:059 · Cautions about practice

    The conflict between the secondary design description and METR's checked methodology cautions against using the wrong work-unit denominator or randomization unit in adoption measurement. Preserve 246 issues and issue-level assignment with developers in both conditions; this mapping adds no full-paper audit or replication.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundaryP052 says 136 issues and implies assignment by developer. METR’s primary methodology reports 246 issues and issue-level randomization, with developers working in both conditions. Do not reproduce the secondary account’s conflicting design description. A primary abstract/methodology check was performed, not a full-paper audit or statistical replication. This is a retitled Pulse excerpt; preserve its existing series provenance. Public availability does not imply an independent check of every paragraph or chart. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Recorded summary. Discusses METR’s experienced-maintainer experiment and possible workflow explanations. A targeted primary-source check confirms 16 developers and 246 issues randomized by issue to AI allowed or disallowed, not separate developer treatment groups.

Reported findings / argument. The primary study reports slower completion in this specific early-2025 setting. P052’s broader all-tools inference and proposed familiarity explanation remain interpretations; neither is independent causal validation.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — secondary research commentary

Editorial use. This is secondary commentary on W023, not a replication; the all-tools extrapolation and causal learning-curve explanation are unsupported.

The source follows one pseudonymous candidate across companies; it does not validate an explainability test or represent independent samples of candidates.

New trend: programming by kicking off parallel AI agents

Discusses concurrent coding-agent workflows through practitioner accounts, contrasting parallel task execution with the serial attention needed to review and land changes.

What agents can doEngineering structure

Related practices

PAT:056 Parallel Work OrchestrationIllustrates practice · primary reading
Why these practices (1)
  • PAT:056 · Illustrates practice

    Practitioner accounts illustrate concurrent agent execution alongside serial review and integration attention, exposing the coordination boundary a parallel workflow must respect. The reused Sid Bidasaria conversation from P062 is dependent reporting, not another independent case.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundaryExcerpt of Pulse #149; shares that issue, not the content of the separate interview-comparison article. This non-Pulse-titled blog article is an excerpt of a Pulse issue originally published 2025-10-09. It passes the literal title-prefix rule; it is excluded by the optional stricter Pulse-origin filter. The parent issue is provenance only, not another P article. The public account explicitly reuses the Sid Bidasaria conversation reported in P062. It is a different article, not independent interview evidence. Public availability does not imply an independent check of every paragraph or chart. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Reported findings / argument. Suggests task partitioning and coordination skills may matter more as agents multiply. Benefits and cognitive costs are hypotheses rather than measured comparative outcomes.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — reported practice commentary

Editorial use. Parallel agent dispatch creates coordination and verification demands; number of agents is not proof of productivity.

P084Pragmatic EngineerIn the published NDSE2 bibliographypublic text

I replaced a $120/year micro-SaaS in 20 minutes with LLM-generated code

Gergely Orosz · 2026-01-29

Reports rebuilding a small testimonials feature with Codex, including planning, modular data, testing and deployment.

EconomicsProductivity

Related practices

PAT:046 Small Verifiable ChunksIllustrates practice · primary readingPAT:060 Cost ManagementCautions about practice
Why these practices (2)
  • PAT:046 · Illustrates practice

    Rebuilding the personal testimonials feature illustrates bounding generated work to a specific function with planning and checks. The scope is the functionality the author used, not the complete SaaS product, and the account is not an independent verification of the resulting software.

    Explore this practice with its sources →
  • PAT:060 · Cautions about practice

    The unmeasured maintenance and opportunity costs caution against treating the subscription price and coding time as the complete economics of the replacement. This personal case cannot establish a general cost advantage for generated substitutes.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundaryThe reported replacement covers the personal functionality the author used, not the complete SaaS product; lifecycle maintenance and opportunity costs were not measured. Public availability does not imply an independent check of every paragraph or chart. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Recorded summary. Reports rebuilding a small testimonials feature with Codex, including planning, modular data, testing and deployment. The replacement covered a narrower personal use case than the original service.

Reported findings / argument. Demonstrates a bounded build-versus-buy example, not the general replacement of SaaS. Maintenance, verification and changing compliance obligations remain outside the headline time comparison.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — first person case report

Editorial use. The personal build-versus-buy experiment has a narrow scope; the headline omits long-term maintenance and service equivalence.

    The reported company-local scoring of AI review tools evaluates one component used to choose a review route: the usefulness of tool findings in that company's trial. P089Pragmatic EngineerIn the published NDSE2 bibliographypublic article paid extras

AI Tooling for Software Engineers in 2026

Gergely Orosz; Elin Nilsson · 2026-03-03

A survey of newsletter readers examines coding-tool adoption, model preferences, seniority and organizational differences.

ProductivityEngineering structure

Related practices

PAT:059 Measurement & LearningCautions about practice · primary reading
Why these practices (1)
  • PAT:059 · Cautions about practice

    The shared 906-response cohort, unmatched survey waves and unresolved 55%/507-person discrepancy caution against mixing denominators or treating usage as longitudinal improvement. The association supports careful adoption measurement, not a new recount or correction of the publisher's data.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundarySurvey ran January 27–February 17, 2026; same cohort as the two impact follow-ups. The author reports 906 responses for the shared 2026 cohort. This is not an independently counted sample; comparisons with other survey waves are not a matched longitudinal panel. The same page calls the paid supplement 65 pages near the beginning and 35 pages near the end. It also pairs 55% regular agent usage with 507 people; 507/906 is about 56%, so the response denominator or rounding needs clarification. Neither discrepancy is silently corrected. Public availability does not imply an independent check of every paragraph or chart. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Reported findings / argument. The volunteer survey reports associations among tool use, role, company size and sentiment. Procurement explanations are author hypotheses, not identified causes; neither population market share nor causal productivity follows from these responses.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — reader survey analysis

Editorial use. The reader survey measures reported usage and sentiment, not causal productivity or population-wide adoption.

Skills & learningCode quality & security

PAT:050 Learning Loop PreservationInforms practice · primary reading
Why these practices (1)
  • PAT:050 · Informs practice

    The survey's separate accounts of less-experienced engineers, focus and cognitive load inform asking what independent reasoning should remain visible during adoption. Subjective reports from the shared 2026 cohort do not demonstrate retained learning or causal skill change.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundarySelf-selected respondents and subjective reports; shared 2026 survey dataset with AI Tooling 2026 and key trends Part 1. The author reports 906 responses for the shared 2026 cohort. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Recorded summary. The final analysis of the publication’s 2026 reader survey examines team adoption, codebase quality, less-experienced engineers and differing experiences of focus and cognitive load. It argues that existing engineering practices shape perceived benefits.

Reported findings / argument. Self-reported benefits coexist with maintenance and learning concerns. This is another analysis of the same survey cohort, not an independent replication of its earlier installments.

Practice classification

Outside the operational-practice scope. Job listings and workforce profiles describe geographic and employer demand. The retained preview does not identify a concrete engineering workflow or enablement procedure.

The record remains in the Atlas. This disposition concerns its fit to the operational practices, not its overall quality or relevance.

Review scope and coverage →
Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundary Subscriber-only article remainder not reviewed. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Recorded summary. The report uses job listings and workforce profiles to examine software and AI engineering demand across countries and employers. The preview explicitly asks whether AI roles are replacing traditional software roles.

Reported findings / argument. The article states that the available data cannot answer replacement causally. Geography, employer coverage and the difference between posted vacancies and employment matter.

Editorial use. The market report combines heterogeneous indicators and requires separating correlation, coverage and causation.

P109Pragmatic Engineerpaid preview

Tech jobs market in 2026, part 3: hiring managers & job seekers

Gergely Orosz · 2026-07-07

Accounts from hiring managers and job seekers describe noisy applications, distrust of AI-enhanced credentials and sharply different demand across specialties and regions.

Jobs & roles

Practice classification

Outside the operational-practice scope. The retained accounts describe labor demand and distrust of AI-enhanced credentials but do not specify a candidate-verification or learning intervention that can be mapped responsibly.

The record remains in the Atlas. This disposition concerns its fit to the operational practices, not its overall quality or relevance.

Review scope and coverage →
Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundary Subscriber-only article remainder not reviewed. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Recorded summary. Accounts from hiring managers and job seekers describe noisy applications, distrust of AI-enhanced credentials and sharply different demand across specialties and regions. This complements, rather than duplicates, the series’ vacancy-data analyses.

Reported findings / argument. Reported hiring friction can coexist with hard-to-fill positions. Interview accounts cannot estimate the industry-wide employment effect of AI or eliminate selection bias.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — qualitative industry interviews

Editorial use. Labor-market interviews describe recruitment signals and uneven opportunities; AI is one contextual factor, not an isolated causal effect or a measured software-development intervention.

What is “loop engineering?”

Gergely Orosz · 2026-07-14

Orosz traces Ralph-style loops, scheduled triggers and goal-oriented harness features.

What agents can doEngineering structure

Related practices

PAT:023 The External Bash LoopInforms practice · primary reading
Why these practices (1)
  • PAT:023 · Informs practice

    The account of Ralph-style loops and scheduled harness features informs considering an external controller for repeated goal-oriented work. The discussed Osmani blog edition is the same underlying work catalogued as O012; paid details and comparative loop outcomes remain unreviewed.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundaryP110 directly links https://addyosmani.com/blog/loop-engineering/ (7 June 2026). O012 catalogues the substantially matching Substack edition (8 June 2026). Treat the edge as discussion of the same underlying work via an alternate edition, not an exact-URL citation. The paid remainder and comparative loop outcomes remain unreviewed. Subscriber-only article remainder not reviewed. No microdata replication, controlled product test, or independent-rater agreement study was performed.

Recorded summary. Orosz traces Ralph-style loops, scheduled triggers and goal-oriented harness features. Developer accounts include useful maintenance automation alongside drift, token spending and disappointment with unnecessary orchestration.

Reported findings / argument. The article questions whether custom loops remain useful as harnesses absorb them. Context design, bounded scope and measurable benefit are more defensible than assuming that more looping improves results.

Source type, as recorded: Industry/practitioner publication — reported practitioner analysis

Editorial use. The critique challenges unnecessary custom orchestration, not the need for bounded execution, context and independent assurance.

What is happening with code reviews?

Gergely Orosz · 2026-09-08

The article surveys responses to growing AI-generated review workloads: reviewing AI feedback, routing by blast radius, inspecting plans and tests, reducing patch size, and retaining manual review.

Verification & reviewEngineering structure

Related practices

PAT:052 Review GauntletInforms practice · primary readingPAT:010 Inference-Healed Code ReviewInforms practicePAT:046 Small Verifiable ChunksInforms practice
Why these practices (3)
  • PAT:052 · Informs practice

    Routing by blast radius and retaining manual review inform selecting a proportionate review path as generated workloads grow. The preview surveys possible responses and does not establish a universally effective sequence of review stages.

    Explore this practice with its sources →
  • PAT:010 · Informs practice

    The requirement to review AI feedback informs treating generated findings as hypotheses to check before initiating a repair. The preview does not establish that acting on an AI comment improves the candidate or that reviewer agreement is independent evidence.

    Explore this practice with its sources →
  • PAT:046 · Informs practice

    Reducing patch size informs choosing a coherent reviewable increment when generated changes exceed reviewer attention. The proposal does not supply an optimal line-count threshold or show that smaller patches remove cross-cutting dependencies.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

What’s the ROI of software engineers’ spending on AI?

Gergely Orosz · 2026-10-20 · Publisher metadata updated 2026-10-21

Reporting from 27 workplaces, combined with CodeRabbit and Gitar aggregates, describes wide variation in AI spending and changes in pull-request throughput. Public examples include higher spending with little throughput change as well as large output increases. The piece supplies practitioner context for spending limits and for measuring benefits beyond PR counts; it does not establish a causal return on AI spending.

ProductivityEconomics

Related practices

PAT:059 Measurement & LearningCautions about practice · primary readingPAT:060 Cost ManagementInforms practice
Why these practices (2)
  • PAT:059 · Cautions about practice

    The contrast between spending and PR throughput cautions against making output volume the benefit measure for AI adoption. The public sections combine nonrandom workplace reports and vendor aggregates; they do not identify causal or quality-adjusted gains.

    Explore this practice with its sources →
  • PAT:060 · Informs practice

    Wide variation in AI spending informs making local cost boundaries and accepted-value assumptions explicit before setting a budget or claiming a return. Only sections 1–3 and introductory material support this link; paid company details and the final ROI discussion were not reconstructed.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

P126Pragmatic EngineerRestricted primary preview

AI SRE: what is it, how could it change on-call – and does it work?

Gergely Orosz; Jessica Salmon · 2026-10-27 · Publisher metadata updated 2026-10-29

Interviews with Rootly, incident.io and ResolveAI describe agents that gather incident context, investigate hypotheses and support engineers in collaboration tools. Public sections distinguish investigation from autonomous remediation, explain service graphs and memory, and discuss data-access and trust constraints. The piece illustrates operational agent design rather than independently benchmarking these tools.

Engineering structureVerification & reviewSystem knowledge & memory

Related practices

PAT:029 Memory and Retrieval: Read What the Model Could Not KnowIllustrates practice · primary readingPAT:034 Safety and Guardrails: Verification Is Not AuthorizationInforms practice
Why these practices (2)
  • PAT:029 · Illustrates practice

    Vendor accounts of service graphs, memory and incident-context gathering illustrate retrieving operational information that an agent cannot infer reliably from its immediate prompt. The public preview is not an independent accuracy or speed benchmark, and the incident.io investment remains disclosed.

    Explore this practice with its sources →
  • PAT:034 · Informs practice

    The public distinction between investigation and autonomous remediation informs treating diagnosis and permission to change production as separate decisions. The interviews do not demonstrate enforcement, and subscriber sections on later operational outcomes were not reviewed.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundaryVendor interviews and reported examples, with no independent tool evaluation. Orosz discloses an investment in incident.io. Only the public preview was reviewed; subscriber sections on accuracy, speed, cost and later operational outcomes were not accessed.

P127Pragmatic EngineerPrimary text checked

How software engineering is changing: a tale of two eras

Neil Kakkar (guest essay); Gergely Orosz, Jessica Salmon and Ivan Klaric (editorial byline) · 2026-11-03

Neil Kakkar compares his own work at an AI-native startup with earlier employers and reports roughly eleven times as many merged PRs as at his previous startup. Alongside higher output, his account describes production errors, context-switching fatigue and loss of shared knowledge as review practices and ownership change. Editorial commentary distinguishes iteration speed from business results.

ProductivityEngineering structureVerification & reviewSystem knowledge & memory

Related practices

PAT:059 Measurement & LearningCautions about practice · primary readingPAT:052 Review GauntletCautions about practice
Why these practices (2)
  • PAT:059 · Cautions about practice

    Neil Kakkar's higher merged-PR output alongside errors and changed work practices cautions against treating roughly elevenfold PR counts as causal productivity. Different employers, roles and products confound the comparison; linked data were not independently recomputed.

    Explore this practice with its sources →
  • PAT:052 · Cautions about practice

    The guest account's review changes, ownership changes and context-switching fatigue inform checking whether review capacity can sustain higher output. It is a single-person retrospective, not a validated recommendation to remove or standardize review stages.

    Explore this practice with its sources →

Primary reading is the main classification for this record, not a strength-of-evidence score. Associations use retained Atlas annotations; they add no manuscript citation or claim that the complete practice was validated.

Evidence, context & provenance
Evidence boundarySingle-person retrospective across different employers, roles, products and processes. PR counts and reported comparisons are not causal or quality-adjusted productivity estimates. Underlying data and linked charts were not independently recomputed; the practices described are not universally validated recommendations.

Source type, as recorded: Self-report / commercial evidence
